title: Ki Teitzei: pay today (Deuteronomy 24:14–15)
hookLine: don't hold a poor worker's wages overnight

cards: For a lot of people, payday decides what's for dinner. A delivery driver waiting on a platform to release last week's earnings. A freelancer chasing an invoice that's sixty days late.
A day laborer outside a hardware store at six in the morning, hoping the cash comes at the end of the shift and not next Friday. For the person paying, a delay is a line on a to-do list.
For the person waiting, it's groceries, or not. The Torah draws the line at sunset.

teach.b: First, the Torah says, don't oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether one of your own people or a stranger living in your towns.
Then the rule, in the old Jewish translation: "In the same day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it."

Leviticus says it too, from the other side of the clock: don't keep a worker's wages overnight until morning. The rabbis called this prohibition bal talin, do not hold it overnight. Now look at the reason.

teach.h: HE LIFTS UP HIS SOUL TO IT.
teach.b: In Hebrew, setteth his heart upon it is closer to: he lifts up his soul to it. His whole self is hanging on that pay.

teach.h: HE CLIMBED, HUNG, RISKED HIS LIFE.
teach.b: The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, reads those words and asks: why did this worker climb the high ramp, hang from the tree, risk his life? For his wages.
So holding back what he earned, the Talmud says, is as if you've taken his life. Strong language for a late payment. But it's the worker's view.
The one who pays sees an amount. The one who's paid sees a day of his life, already spent, waiting to come back as bread.
The verse ends with a warning: or he will cry to the LORD against you, and it will be counted as sin.

how: Jewish law forbids delaying payment to workers past the agreed time, called bal talin, and observant employers, from families paying a babysitter to businesses, are taught to pay day workers by the end of the day or night they worked.

games.q: a day laborer finishes work at sunset. you'll be at the bank tomorrow anyway. what does Deuteronomy say?
o: pay tomorrow; one night won't matter.
pay him the same day, before the sun goes down.
pay at the end of the month with everyone else.
games.why: in the same day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it.

practice: Think of what you owe that's sitting on your list: not just bills, but the babysitter, the friend who covered lunch, the kid down the street who mowed the lawn.
Picture the person on the other end, not the amount, and what they're waiting to do with it. Let one of them stay with you while the sun is still up.

wordCard.voice: Ki Teitzei. When you go out. The portion where a worker's pay can't wait past sundown.

orig.note: Hebrew: in his day you shall give his wage. the opening of Deuteronomy 24:15.

carryVoice: Your line: pay today. To the one who waits, it's a day of his life. That's day five hundred nine.
